title: Sirocco consumer banking – mixed-workload burst profiling brief
content:
Objective:
Summarize results from a 10-day mixed-workload burst profiling run for Sirocco (consumer banking chatbot). Goal: quantify tail-latency, throughput, and incremental token cost across operational modes the customer expects in production: interactive low-latency chat (latency-sensitive) plus periodic batch enrichment jobs (throughput-oriented). Deliverables: recommendation for Dedicated capacity sizing, fallback policies, caching and quantization knobs to meet p95 latency <= 350 ms for interactive flows while minimizing overall token cost.

Background and context:
Sirocco is a mid-sized digital banking platform expecting mixed traffic: 60% interactive conversational queries (avg user prompt 40 tokens, expected model output 90 tokens) and 40% periodic enrichment calls (batch document embeddings and summarization with longer inputs, avg 1200 input tokens, output 400 tokens). Traffic pattern is diurnal with abrupt bursts (marketing pushes) and microbursts related to account reconciliation jobs. Customer constraint: no more than 2x increase in monthly inference spend during peak campaign windows; SLO for interactive p95 350 ms. They prefer Dedicated pools but are open to hybrid fallback into hosted lower‑cost variants.

Test matrix and environment:
- Date range: 2029-12-03 to 2029-12-05 (intensive sweeps), follow-up runs on 2029-12-06
- Hardware: Dedicated pool using A800x8 (32GB GPUs) for primary runs; comparison runs on A100-40GB and a cheaper T4-like GPU for fallback cost calculations.
- Models tested: "robin-7b" (FP16 baseline), "robin-7b-awq-int8" (AWQ static int8), "robin-13b-fp16" (higher quality), plus a distilled 3b variant for cheap fallback.
- Serving config variables: batch size caps (1, 4, 16), max-seq limits (512/2048), KV cache enabled/disabled, prefix caching warm/cold, and dynamic batching latency target setpoints (50ms/100ms/200ms).
- Workloads: mixed traffic generator synthesized from production trace (anonymized). Burst scenarios: 4x baseline for 5 mins, 8x microburst for 30s, sustained 2x for 2 hours. Background batch jobs run concurrently at fixed windows.

Key metrics captured:
- p50/p90/p95/p99 server-side generation latency (ms) for interactive flows
- tokens/sec and completed requests/sec for enrichment jobs
- GPU utilization and queue depth distribution
- effective cost per 1M tokens (including Dedicated amortized pool cost)
- cold vs warm cache delta
- fallback frequency and success rate when using cheaper variant as overflow

Representative results (high level):
1) Interactive baseline (robin-7b FP16)
   - steady-state (no burst): p50 42 ms, p95 220 ms, p99 410 ms, throughput ~140 req/s (40/90 token profile)
   - 4x burst (5 mins): p95 increases to 520 ms when batch cap=16 and dynamic latency setpoint 200 ms; with batch cap=4 and setpoint=50 ms p95 held at 330 ms but throughput dropped ~18% and queue tailing increased (higher rejection/backpressure).

2) AWQ quantized variant (robin-7b-awq-int8)
   - steady-state: p50 38 ms, p95 195 ms, quality degradation measured as small decrease on BLEU/ROUGE-like evals for summarization (~1.6% score delta vs FP16 baseline)
   - burst behavior: better queueing headroom, p95 observed 420 ms at 8x microburst (vs 700+ ms for FP16 on same config).

3) Heavy enrichment jobs (robin-13b-fp16)
   - throughput: 340 tokens/sec per GPU for long sequences (avg 1600 tokens total).
   - when co-located with interactive traffic on same GPU pool without strict isolation, interactive p95 degraded by ~2.1x.

4) Cold vs warm cache impact
   - Cold-start (after idle >30 mins): median extra 85 ms due to KV cache cold misses for interactive flows.
   - Prefix caching of common onboarding prompts reduced average output tokens by ~6% (less hallucination loops) and improved effective p95 by ~12% for first-turn flows.

5) Cost modeling (monthlyized for customer projected 1.2B tokens/month)
   - Baseline Dedicated FP16-only: estimated $38k/month (infrastructure + reserved capacity amortized)
   - Mixed mode (primary AWQ quantized for interactive + robin-13b for enrichment in dedicated but scheduled off-peak): estimated $26k/month (-32%) while meeting p95 <= 350 ms in 93% of interactive windows (exceptions at highest microbursts).
   - Fallback policy that routes excess to cheaper hosted-distilled 3b reduces peak spend but increases p95 failures to 12% during highest microbursts. Net cost $22k/month but requires SLO relaxation or user-facing degradation.

Observations and tradeoffs:
- Quantization (AWQ int8) gave the best win for mixed-workloads: lower latency, improved headroom during bursts, modest quality cost. This is the most cost-effective knob.
- Strict co-location of heavy batch enrichment with latency-sensitive interactive traffic on the same physical GPUs risks violating p95 when not using strict request shaping or isolation. Recommendation: schedule enrichment on separate capacity or enforce strong priority routing.
- Dynamic batching must be tuned conservatively for this customer: a latency target of 50–100 ms preserves p95 goals at cost of some throughput; 200 ms increases overall token efficiency but risks exceeding SLO during microbursts.
- Cache warmup matters: pre-warming KV caches before marketing campaigns materially reduces tail. We observed ~85 ms median penalty otherwise.
- Fallback to a smaller distilled model is an effective cost-safety valve but degrades quality; use as last-resort only with graceful messaging / user fallback UX.

Recommendations (concise):
1) Run Dedicated pool with AWQ quantized robin-7b for interactive traffic (pin this model).
2) Isolate enrichment jobs to a separate Dedicated pool sized for burst windows (use autoscale with admission control and job queueing).
3) Configure dynamic batching setpoint = 75 ms for interactive route, batch cap = 4.
4) Implement prefix caching for the top 20 common onboarding prompts; add a cache pre-warm job prior to expected campaigns.
5) Maintain a distilled 3b hosted fallback route with a circuit-breaker that engages only when queue depth > threshold; surface clear metrics and runbook for degraded responses.
6) Continue quantization validation on customer eval sets for any AWQ variants and run periodic quality checks (weekly) during the first 6 weeks of production.

Operational runbook (short):
- Pre-campaign checklist: pre-warm KV cache, scale enrichment pool to +25%, disable on-duty model rollouts in the 2-hour prewindow.
- Incident triage (if p95 > 350 ms): check queue depth -> if > 75% thresholds, enable fallback routing and scale interactive pool; if GPU util low but latency high, check batch setpoints and KV cold misses.
- Post-mortem items: correlate p95 spikes with batch job start timestamps and marketing push messages in Slack channel #sirocco-poc.

Open questions & next steps:
- Run a 72-hour production mirror with real user traffic (sanitized) to validate AWQ quality on edge cases (financial instruction disambiguation).
- Explore AWQ + LLM-ops hybrid where short interactive flows use int8 and longer enrichment flows use fp16 within the same autoscaler group but with request priorities.
- Validate cost model with actual reserved capacity contract numbers from finance; the current model uses list prices and our internal amortization assumptions.

Appendix (quick notes):
- Synthetic generator: replayed anonymized event trace from 2029-11 with randomized start-times to create microbursts; preserved user-turn length distribution.
- Eval artifacts: quality eval scripts stored in github:repo/sirocco-poc/eval and output CSV: s3://redwood-temp/sirocco/poc-evals/2029-12/
- Slack summary posted: https://redwood.slack.com/archives/C02SIR0/docs-12345
